questions.q: Define the PEEL structure for oral literary discussion and name its four components in speaking order.
questions.a: PEEL = Point (state your interpretive claim in one sentence), Evidence (cite a specific textual detail — line, image, anecdote), Explanation (analyze how the evidence proves the point, 2-3 sentences), Link (connect back to the chapter's central idea or forward to the next speaker's point). A wrong answer (e.g., "Point, Example, Explain, Conclusion") reveals the student confuses written essay structure with oral discussion flow — oral Link must explicitly invite or acknowledge the next speaker, not just summarize.

questions.q: Create a 90-second opening statement for a discussion on: "Can a river have legal personhood?" Ground it in two chapter concepts and one contemporary Indian case.
questions.a: Strong answer structure: (1) Hook: "Muktibodh calls the river 'voèkwr' — a living tradition, not a resource." (2) Concept 1: River as "ekuorkoknh lkfgR;dkj" (humanistic litterateur) — implies agency, voice, rights. (3) Concept 2: River as "iqjkus iQyksa dk dksey ncko" (historian of layered pasts) — legal personhood protects this archive. (4) Case: 2017 Uttarakhand HC declaring Ganga-Yamuna legal persons (later stayed by SC) — exactly the "voèkwr" recognition Muktibodh demands. (5) Provocation: "If a corporation can be a legal person, why not a river that 'jkLrk lekIr gks x;k' (became whole) over millennia?" Weak answers omit the textual grounding or treat the case as decoration — revealing inability to bridge literary concept and civic argument.
